blocks.text: The Record of Lord Yu Jingyi Meeting the Kitchen God — Vernacular Text

inline.s: In the Jiajing era of the Ming dynasty there lived in Jiangxi a Lord Yu, whose personal name was Du and whose courtesy name was Liangchen, a man of wide learning and many talents. At the age of eighteen he passed the examination and became a licensed scholar, and in every test at the county school he invariably ranked among the first.

By the time he reached manhood, however, his family had fallen into poverty, and he made his living by teaching. Together with more than ten fellow students of the county school he formed a Wenchang Society, observing the teachings of Lord Wenchang: to cherish written characters, to release living creatures, to abstain from lust, to abstain from killing, and to abstain from faults of speech. In this practice he persevered for many years.

Yet he sat for the provincial examination seven times, one after another, and never once passed. He had five sons, four of whom died of illness in childhood. Only the third remained, a boy of rare intelligence and beauty, with a pair of moles on the sole of his left foot. Husband and wife treasured him as a jewel, but at the age of eight, while playing about the neighborhood, he was lost. Of four daughters, only one was raised. Because of the children who died young and the son who was lost, his wife wept until both her eyes went blind. Lord Yu dragged out his years in poverty and dejection, and his lot grew worse with every passing day.

Lord Yu examined himself and judged that he had committed no great fault, and yet had bitterly suffered the punishment of Heaven. From his fortieth year onward, on every New Year’s Eve, he would write a petition on yellow paper and pray to the Kitchen God, beseeching him to report to the Jade Emperor the case of a man who had “committed no great fault, yet bitterly suffered the punishment of Heaven.” He did so for several years, and there was no answer.

In his forty-seventh year, on New Year’s Eve, Lord Yu sat through the night with his blind wife and their one daughter. The whole house was cold and bare, and they kept one another company in desolation, a sorrow too heavy to bear. Suddenly they heard a knock at the door, and Lord Yu took up a candle to open it. There stood a gentleman in a black robe and a scholar’s cap, his beard and hair half grey. After exchanging a deep bow, he took a seat and introduced himself: “My surname is Zhang. I have just returned from a long journey, and hearing the mournful sighs of your household, I have come especially to offer you comfort.” Lord Yu was astonished at the man’s arrival and treated him with the greatest respect. He then told him his whole story: how all his life he had studied and learned much and had accumulated many good deeds, yet for thirty years he had sat for the provincial examination and to this day had never passed; how of his children some had died and one had been lost; how his wife had wept her eyes blind; and how the family could scarcely keep itself in food and clothing. And he read aloud to Zhang each of the petitions he had burned in prayer to the Kitchen God.

Zhang said: “I have known of your family’s affairs for a long time. The evil of your mind is far too heavy, and you devote yourself solely to empty reputation. Moreover, your petitions are filled with resentment and rancor, irreverently laid before the Jade Emperor. I fear the punishment you receive will not stop here!”

Lord Yu was greatly startled and said: “I have heard that in the unseen realm even the smallest good deed is surely recorded. I have vowed to practice good deeds, and for many years I have reverently and scrupulously kept the rules of the Wenchang Society. Can it all have been good in name only?”

Zhang said: “The truth of the matter is not as you say. Take the rule you observe of cherishing written characters. Your students and your friends often use pages of books, essays, and old paper volumes to paper windows and wrap parcels, and even to wipe tables, and then, on the pretext of not defiling them, they burn them. You see this with your own eyes every day and never once so much as warn them; you merely pick up written paper you happen to see in the street, carry it home, and burn it. What good does that do?

When your society releases living creatures each month, you do no more than bustle along with the others, drifting with the current. If no one takes the initiative, you simply let the matter rest; in truth, no thought of compassion has ever arisen from within your own heart.
And in your own household, shrimps, crabs, and the like are boiled and eaten. You say you abstain from killing — are they alone not living beings?

Then there is the rule against faults of speech. Your words are quick and clever, and those who hear you are often filled with admiration. When you speak, you know in your own heart that you are wounding kindness, yet when you talk with relatives and close friends about people or affairs, you are forever mocking, jeering, and cutting at them, and you cannot restrain yourself. Your tongue is like a sharp blade: frivolous, cruel, and slanderous, and wherever its edge falls it stirs the anger of gods and spirits. The underworld long ago recorded these evil deeds of yours in its registers, and there is no knowing how many there are — yet you still set yourself up as a plain and generous man. Search your heart: whom do you mean to deceive? Heaven?

the rule against lust: although you have committed no actual deed of sexual misconduct, whenever you see another man’s beautiful daughter you gaze at her long and steadily, and your mind sways and cannot be stilled. It is only that no illicit occasion has ever come together for you. Ask yourself in turn: if she were to knock at your door at night, could you, like the chaste man of Lu, shut the door and refuse her? Yet you claim that in all your life you have committed no sexual misconduct, and that you can face Heaven, Earth, and the gods and spirits. That is absurdity at its very extreme!
These are the very rules you vowed to keep strictly, and you have not truly kept a single one of them — to say nothing of the rest!

The petitions you have burned over the years have all been delivered on high. The Jade Emperor commanded the Day-Wandering Envoys to observe your good and evil for several years, and there was not one good deed to record. All they saw was that when you were alone in private, thoughts of greed, thoughts of lust, thoughts of envy, thoughts of petty resentment, thoughts of exalting yourself and belittling others, thoughts of brooding over the past and longing for the future, thoughts of expecting others to repay your kindness, and thoughts of taking revenge for yourself came and went in your mind without end. These manifold evils of the mind are firmly knotted within you; the gods have recorded them in abundance, and Heaven’s punishment will grow heavier and heavier. You will not even have time to escape disaster — by what right do you still ask Heaven to send down blessings?

Astonished and terrified, Lord Yu knelt on the ground with tears streaming down his face and said: “Since you, sir, know the affairs of the unseen realm, you must be a venerable deity. I beg you, save me and show me a way to live.”

Zhang said: “You are a man of learning who understands propriety, and you too admire good conduct. When you hear a fine saying, you are stirred and encouraged; when you see a good deed, you cannot help but be inspired. But after a little while you forget it. This is because the root of your faith was never deep, and so your virtue cannot endure. Thus the good words and good deeds of your whole life have been nothing but drifting along with the crowd and going through the motions — when was even one of them done in solid earnest? And with your heart full of evil intent, rising and falling, winding on and on, you still ask Heaven to grant you the finest rewards. That is like planting thorns over the whole countryside and then foolishly dreaming of harvesting fine grain — is it not utterly mistaken?

From this day on, whenever thoughts of greed, of lust, of violence, or of delusion and other stray thoughts arise, first sweep them all away with fierce resolve and clear them out completely, so that every thought turns toward the side of good alone. If there is a good deed within your power to do, do it without seeking reward and without seeking fame; whether great or small, difficult or easy, do it in solid earnest, open and unburdened, with patience. If it lies beyond your power, then strive diligently all the same, so that this good intention may be brought to perfection. First, you must have the mind of patience; second, you must have the mind of perseverance. Never let yourself slacken; never deceive yourself. Practice this long and steadily, and you will naturally obtain effects beyond anything you could imagine.

household has served me with great devotion, and so I have come especially to tell you these things. You must quickly do your utmost to carry them out, and only then can the will of Heaven be turned.” Having said this, Zhang walked into an inner room. Lord Yu rose and followed him, but when they reached the kitchen stove he suddenly vanished. Only then did Lord Yu understand that he was the Kitchen God, and he burned incense and bowed his thanks.

In those first days of cutting off evil and practicing good, stray thoughts rose in swarms and stole in through every opening: now he hesitated in doubt and could not go forward, now he grew lazy and slack and could not rouse his spirits. Time passed swiftly, and he remained exactly as he had been. And so, before the image of Guanyin enshrined in his family hall, Lord Yu knocked his head on the ground until it bled and solemnly made his vow: “May my good thoughts remain forever pure and my good efforts advance ever more vigorously. blocks.text: 6. Accumulating Blessings and Turning Heaven’s Will

inline.s: In Lord Yu’s fiftieth year — the second year of the Wanli reign — the metropolitan examination was held, and provincial graduates from all over the country came to the capital to sit for the jinshi degree. At that time Zhang Jiangling was Senior Grand Secretary, the equivalent of a chancellor, directing the great affairs of the Grand Secretariat. After the examination was over, he went to visit the men of Jiangxi who had come to the capital for it, hoping to choose for his sons a tutor of excellent character and learning. Everyone with one voice recommended Lord Yu. Zhang Jiangling accordingly engaged him to come to the capital as a family tutor, and Lord Yu set out with his household.

Zhang Jiangling held Lord Yu’s moral cultivation in high esteem and, citing existing precedent, approved his admission to the Imperial Academy. In the fourth year of Wanli, Lord Yu sat for the provincial examination in the capital and passed as a juren; the following year he passed as a jinshi.

One day Lord Yu went to call on the eunuch Lord Yang. Lord Yang had long heard of Lord Yu’s virtue and learning, and he summoned all five of his sons to come and pay their respects. These boys he had selected and bought from all parts of the country to be his heirs and to gladden his old age. One of them was sixteen years old, and Lord Yu found his features strangely familiar; he asked him where he was from. The boy answered: “I am from Jiangxi. When I was small I strayed onto a grain transport boat and was carried away from my home village, and even now I seem to remember my original surname and the look of my old neighborhood in the lanes.” He then described everything in detail. When Lord Yu had heard him out he was greatly astonished, and he had the boy take off the shoe and sock from his left foot. There he saw the pair of moles on the sole, just as they had been in his childhood. Lord Yu cried out in a loud voice: “You are my son!”

Lord Yang was astonished as well and at once sent the boy home with Lord Yu. Lord Yu hurried to tell his wife. She felt her son with her hands and wept aloud, tears of blood streaming down. The boy too wept without ceasing; he took his mother’s face in both hands and licked her blind eyes with his tongue, and suddenly his mother’s eyes regained their sight.

Grief and joy mingled in Lord Yu’s heart. He had no wish for office; he took leave of Zhang Jiangling and returned to his native place. Zhang Jiangling greatly admired this true and sincere affection, and gave him generous gifts to speed him on his way. When Lord Yu came home, he devoted himself to good works more wholeheartedly than ever. His son married and in time had seven children, all of whom were raised; they were able to carry on the family calling and were fond of study and learning.

Lord Yu wrote down with his own hand the story of his encounter with the Kitchen God and his own practice of reform, in order to instruct his descendants. He enjoyed health and long life, living to the age of eighty-eight, and passed away without illness. People all said: this was the reward of practicing good and turning back the will of
